I believe adaptive sensing and conservative sample-return reserves matter most, so I’m adding fault-aware navigation, targeted site searches, and explicit docking logic.

attempts.hypothesis: I assume GPS, compass, wheel feedback and rays are the only reliable initial senses, so the rover will calibrate its pose online, use conservative reactive obstacle avoidance, search each high-value hint with a science-gradient-assisted circle, and return/dock before energy or time runs out.

I will use a conservative adaptive differential-drive controller that builds a local obstacle grid, follows GPS/compass/odometry fusion, searches hints with a short expanding spiral, samples opportunistically, and returns/charges based on measured energy and time margins.

I will use a simple, robust reactive controller with GPS/odometry pose estimation, hint-centered circular searching, local site-bearing tracking, and adaptive energy/time return margins instead of heavyweight mapping that can fail at startup.

I’ll prioritize never destroying the rover: cap actual speed below the crash threshold, use conservative ray-based avoidance, adaptive wheel-speed control, short searches around hints, and return/dock with measured energy and time margins.

I’m keeping the rover deliberately slow, using measured wheel-speed feedback with hard caps, reactive ray clearance and bump escape instead of aggressive path planning, and returning after each sample so any successful pickup is safely delivered.

I’m keeping the rover deliberately slow but making it fault-aware: stuck low range readings are detected and ignored, a coarse persistent map plus A* avoids local minima, and the planner prioritizes quick round trips to nearby valued hints while sampling opportunistically and returning before time/e

I’ll trade the previous ultra-cautious driving for a measured but much faster feedback controller, using GPS/odometry/compass fusion, short rectangular searches around hints, science-signal false-positive rejection, opportunistic sampling, and explicit return/charge margins.

I’ll stop relying on reactive obstacle dodging alone: this controller builds a persistent local occupancy map, plans on it periodically, caps real wheel speed below the crash threshold, uses detours to escape local minima, and conservatively samples/returns before time or energy risks.

I assume the sites are sparse and value-weighted, the compass has an unknown bias, and the battery and sand costs are unknown, so this controller learns heading bias and energy per metre online, visits hints by value per distance, searches around each hint, and returns to dock when the load, battery

Attempt 1 jittered against a rock and hit it at 1.1 m/s, so this rewrite caps forward speed near rocks, uses ray-based steering and wheel-speed stuck detection with timed escapes, learns the compass bias from GPS straight runs, spirals around hints to find sites, and returns home with a time margin.

Both earlier runs pinned the rover against a ridge or rock while it kept driving into it, so this version uses ray-based obstacle avoidance with speed caps near obstacles, stuck and bump escapes, dead reckoning through GPS freezes, and a hint search that sweeps a 14 m ring.

Attempts 1 to 3 delivered nothing because the rover pinned on rocks and got lost on the way back, so this version builds an occupancy grid from the rays, plans A* routes around it, and delivers in batches while watching time and battery.

Attempt 4 lost 25 value of samples because a stuck range ray and a spin loop pinned the rover far from base, and a re-drill bug wasted time, so this version ignores frozen rays, detects spin and no-progress stalls, skips sites it has already sampled, and uses science-signal pseudo-hints to find site

Attempt 5 delivered only 19 because the rover wasted most of the mission on slow approaches, long dock trips and a stuck-ray detour, so this version keeps its navigation and adds a fuller hint search (7 m ring, then a peak ring, then a 14 m ring), value-aware docking, and slightly faster speed caps.

The attempt-6 trace shows the rover circling or sitting in sand for hundreds of seconds and then running out of time on a single long dock trip, so this version adds area-based stall detection, an earlier time-based return rule, and shorter hint search limits.

Attempt 7 delivered one 8-value sample after about 700 s of wandering with it on board, so this version docks sooner when no new hint is nearby, shortens hint-search timeouts, and keeps the rest of the attempt-7 navigation unchanged.
